lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- Used to, But Not Anymore
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Bruna Viana da Silva Rocha | Lesson 7 -- Used to, But Not Anymore

listenings.text: I get asked about it at every dinner party, and the question is always the same. Do you miss it. I used to hate that question. Now I think it is the right one. For eleven years I was a nurse. I used to get up at four forty, I used to eat standing up, and I used to know exactly what my Tuesday was going to look like in March. And then one week I did not want to get out of the car in the parking lot. Not once. Four days in a row. That was the whole warning I got. People want a story with a moment in it, something dramatic, and there was not one. There was a parking lot. So do I miss it? I miss being needed that badly. I do not miss the four forty. And I did not use to believe that both of those could be true at the same time, but they are, and nobody warns you about that either.

Everybody tells the story of the person who left. Nobody tells mine, and there are more of me. I did the same job for twenty-six years. Same building for nineteen of them. I used to think that made me boring, and for about a decade I was pretty unhappy about it, because everybody around me was pivoting. That was the word. Everybody was pivoting. And then my daughter asked me, when she was fifteen, whether I liked my job. And I said something I had not planned. I said no, but I like who I am at six o'clock. That is the trade I made. I did not use to be able to say it out loud. Here is my only advice, and it is not advice against leaving. Be honest about what you are buying. Some people buy the work. Some people buy the six o'clock. Both of those cost you the other one, and anybody who tells you otherwise is selling something.
